Neo-Orthodoxy
nee-oh-OR-thuh-dok-see
noun
From Greek neos (new) + orthos (straight, correct) + doxa (opinion, teaching). Coined in the 20th century to describe Karl Barth's dialectical theology and its successors, which sought to recover Reformation categories (grace, revelation, the Word of God) while accepting the historical-critical conclusions that had dismantled 19th-century liberalism.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Neo-orthodoxy is the 20th-century theological movement, associated chiefly with Karl Barth, Emil Brunner, and Reinhold Niebuhr, that reacted against 19th-century liberal theology's reduction of Christianity to moral progress and human religious experience, while retaining the historical-critical approach to Scripture that liberalism had normalized. Neo-orthodoxy speaks of “revelation,” “the Word of God,” and “grace,” giving the impression of orthodoxy. The crucial difference is its doctrine of Scripture: for Barth, the Bible is not the Word of God but becomes the Word of God in the moment of divine encounter. Scripture is a fallible human witness to revelation; revelation itself is an event, not a propositional deposit. This position formally accepts the higher-critical conclusion that the Bible contains historical errors and contradictions while claiming that this does not undermine its theological function. The confessional answer is unambiguous: “All Scripture is God-breathed” (2 Tim. 3:16) describes the text itself, not a subjective encounter with it. “No prophecy of Scripture came about by the prophet's own interpretation” (2 Pet. 1:20)—the text has an objective, stable character because God superintended its production, not merely its reception. Neo-orthodoxy's attractive vocabulary (sovereignty, grace, the Word) masks its decisive concession: that the Bible as a written text is not the inerrant, infallible Word of God and therefore cannot function as the sole, supreme authority in faith and practice that the Reformation confessions affirm.

Origin & Era

Neo-orthodoxy: a 20th-century Protestant theological movement reclaiming Reformation themes (grace, revelation, Word of God) while retaining historical-critical assumptions about Scripture; associated with Karl Barth and dialectical theology.

expand to see more

NEO-OR'THO-DOX-Y, noun. (20th-century coinage.) A theological movement arising in continental Europe after World War I, reacting against liberal theology's moralism and optimism while accepting its critical approach to Scripture.

Distinguished from orthodoxy proper in its denial of biblical inerrancy: the Bible ‘becomes' the Word of God in encounter, rather than being the Word of God as written.

Karl Barth's Church Dogmatics is the movement's defining monument; Emil Brunner and Reinhold Niebuhr represent moderate and American forms respectively.

Neo-orthodoxy recovered the categories of divine sovereignty and human sinfulness from 19th-century liberalism's neglect, while redefining revelation as personal encounter rather than propositional inscription.

Confessional Protestantism (Westminster, 1689 LBCF) stands in direct opposition to neo-orthodoxy on Scripture: the confession affirms the Bible as the very Word of God in written form, inerrant and infallible.

Key Scripture

2 Timothy 3:16 — "All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness,"

2 Peter 1:21 — "For prophecy never had its origin in the human will, but prophets, though human, spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit."

2 Peter 1:20 — "Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture came about by the prophet's own interpretation of things."

John 1:1 — "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."

Modern Corruption

Neo-orthodoxy corrupts orthodoxy by retaining its vocabulary while evacuating its substance—speaking of “the Word of God” while denying that the written text of Scripture is that Word in any stable, propositional sense.

expand to see more

Neo-orthodoxy is perhaps the most sophisticated corruption of Christian doctrine in the 20th century precisely because it uses orthodox language to reach heterodox conclusions. A theologian who affirms “revelation,” “grace,” and “the Word of God” sounds confessional; when those terms are unpacked, revelation is existential encounter, grace is God's personal self-disclosure rather than forensic imputation, and the Word is an event rather than a text. Seminary students trained on Barth absorb the vocabulary without recognizing that the dictionary has been changed. Many evangelicals who followed neo-orthodoxy into its “mediating” positions became the founding generation of what is now called progressive Christianity.

The recovery requires insisting on the specific claim of 2 Timothy 3:16: the text (graphē) itself is theopneustos—God-breathed. Not “the encounter with the text,” not “the apostolic tradition behind the text,” but the written text as received. The analogy is the incarnation: as Christ is fully God and fully man, Scripture is fully the Word of God and fully a human document—without error in the one nature, without loss of humanity in the other. Neo-orthodoxy's Bible is human all the way down, capable of divine encounter but incapable of propositional, authoritative truth. That is not the Bible the confessions confess.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek neos + orthos + doxa names the movement's self-presentation as a new orthodoxy—a claim that itself signals the problem: true orthodoxy needs no prefix.

expand to see more

Greek neos — new, recent; the prefix that signals a departure from historic orthodoxy even while claiming recovery

Greek orthos — straight, correct, right; the standard neo-orthodoxy invoked while redefining what counts as correct doctrine

Greek doxa — opinion, teaching, glory; in theological usage, right teaching (orthodoxia) passed down through the church's confessional tradition

German dialektische Theologie — dialectical theology, the self-designation of Barth's school; God is always the wholly Other encountered in paradox

Greek theopneustos — God-breathed (2 Tim. 3:16); the term that decides what neo-orthodoxy denied: the text's own divine inspiration

Usage

"Neo-orthodoxy's influence on 20th-century seminaries explains much of the doctrinal drift in mainline denominations: students absorbed Barthian categories and graduated with a functionally liberal Scripture doctrine dressed in Reformed language."

"Distinguishing neo-orthodoxy from liberalism is important historically, but for confessional purposes both deny inerrancy—the practical difference is that neo-orthodoxy can deceive evangelicals who would never knowingly accept liberal theology."

"A pastor who speaks confidently of “God's Word” while citing higher-critical scholarship as settling textual questions is likely operating with neo-orthodox assumptions, not confessional ones."
